prompt: What do the letters of the VMYP method stand for?
explanation: VMYP splits each variance into Volume, Mix, Yield (productivity) and Price/cost sub-variances.

prompt: What is "flexible budget 1" in a VMYP analysis?

options.text: The budget adjusted to the actual sales volume, all other amounts (prices included) equal to the budget
The actual results restated at budgeted prices
The budget revised during the year (re-forecast)
The budget of fixed costs only

explanation: Flexible budgets are intermediaries between planned and actual figures. Flexible budget 1 shows what income should have been had the actual volume been anticipated, everything else being equal to the budget.

prompt: Which statements about the VMYP method are correct?

options.text: The total variance equals the sum of all sub-variances
It measures the impact of each cause on income, favourable or unfavourable
It assumes that the causes of variances are independent
It can only be applied to a budget-versus-actual comparison

explanation: Sub-variances add up to the total variance and measure the weight of each cause. One limitation is the assumption of independent causes. The method can also compare two periods of time.

prompt: Costs show an unfavourable volume variance. What does this mean?

options.text: Costs rose mechanically because more units were sold – not necessarily poor cost management
The purchasing department paid higher prices
The fixed costs exceeded the budget

explanation: A volume variance on a cost reflects activity. A favourable volume variance on a cost (lower sales) does not mean the cost was well managed either.

prompt: How are variances on fixed costs mostly interpreted?
explanation: Fixed costs do not vary with volume; a variance is mostly a price/spending variance. It is treated as a volume variance only if the relevant range of activity is exceeded.

prompt: Which are benefits of monitoring results with dashboards rather than with a cost-accounting model?

options.text: It does not rely on the accounting information system
It offers more flexibility in defining the performance model and facilitates learning
Variances can be summed up to obtain the total variance

explanation: Dashboards are faster and more flexible, but there is no mathematical relationship between their variances: they cannot be summed, so ranking them is more subjective.

prompt: Planned: 100 units at €50. Actual: 115 units at €48. What is the selling price variance on turnover?
explanation: (48 − 50) × 115 actual units = −230 € (unfav.). The volume variance on turnover is (115 − 100) × 50 = +750 €.

prompt: In the slide example (planned 100 units, actual 115; material 3.20 kg/unit planned, 3.10 actual, €8.80/kg), what is the yield variance on material cost?
explanation: 115 × (3.10 − 3.20) × 8.80 = −101.2 € on cost → +101 on the production margin (fav.). 36 is the material price variance, 422 the volume variance on variable costs.

prompt: A two-product company sells more of its cheaper product than budgeted, total volume unchanged. Which sales sub-variance is affected first?
explanation: The mix sub-variance compares the actual mix with the budget mix at budgeted prices: a higher share of the cheaper product makes it unfavourable.

statement: The sum of all sub-variances equals the overall variance.
explanation: Total variance = sum of all sub-variances (volume, mix, yield, price, fixed costs).

statement: An overall favourable variance proves that every component of performance was good.
explanation: An overall favourable variance does not prevent poor performance on some sub-variances – it must be broken down.

statement: The volume sub-variance on sales is valued at actual selling prices.
explanation: Volume (and mix) sub-variances are valued at budgeted prices; the difference between actual and budgeted prices is the price sub-variance.

statement: Variance analysis always matches the controllability principle.
explanation: Responsibility for a variance can be shared between departments (e.g. purchasing price vs. production yield), so variance analysis does not always match controllability.

statement: Results analysis can also be applied between two periods of time, not only between budget and actual.
explanation: Its general objectives – monitoring objectives (regulation) and confirming/adjusting the performance model (learning) – also apply to a comparison of two periods.

statement: A favourable yield variance may be linked to an unfavourable material price variance.
explanation: Crossed effects: better-quality (more expensive) material can reduce waste.

statement: One limitation of results monitoring based on a cost-accounting model is its slow response time.
explanation: Limitations: slow response time, focus on causes whose impact on income can be measured, assumption of independent causes.

statement: With dashboards, the variances on the different indicators can be added up to explain the total variance in income.
explanation: There is no mathematical relationship between dashboard variances; they cannot be summed and ranking them is more subjective.

statement: A favourable volume sub-variance on sales can be linked to an unfavourable selling price sub-variance.
explanation: Crossed effect: we may sell more because the selling price is attractive.

prompt: Slide example – planned: 100 units at €50, material 3.20 kg/unit at €8.80/kg, fixed costs €1,000. Actual: 115 units at €48, 3.10 kg/unit at €8.90/kg, fixed costs €1,050. Compute the sub-variances on the production margin (favourable = positive).
modelAnswer: Volume +328 (turnover +750, variable costs −422), yield +101, selling price −230, material price −36, fixed costs −50. Overall +113.2 (production margin 1,297.2 vs 1,184).

steps.title: Volume (flexible budget 1)
steps.why: Actual volume, everything else as budgeted.

prompt: Budget: product A 600 units at €100, product B 400 units at €200. Actual: A 700 units at €98, B 400 units at €205. Compute the volume, mix and price sub-variances on sales.

basis.ref: im Stil von STET Sportswear, Q3

prompt: Explain why an overall favourable variance on income still has to be broken down into sub-variances. Give an example.
modelAnswer: An overall favourable variance can hide unfavourable sub-variances that offset each other (e.g. a favourable volume variance hiding an unfavourable selling price variance, as in the slide example: +750 volume on turnover vs −230 price). Breaking it down identifies the causes, ranks them, reveals crossed effects (selling more because prices were cut) and makes corrective action possible (market study on prices, negotiation of material prices).
keyPoints: Favourable total can hide unfavourable sub-variances
Identify and rank causes, crossed effects
